items.text: A scream recorded for the 1951 film Distant Drums was reused in other films for decades. New sound effects were costly at the time, so studios recycled it.
items.note: Wikipedia says the scream was 'allegedly' voiced by actor Sheb Wooley, so who recorded it is not certain.

items.text: Star Wars sound designer Ben Burtt calls the Wilhelm scream an in-joke that got out of hand. It has ended up in hundreds of films, including Star Wars and Toy Story.

sources.title: How the Wilhelm scream became Hollywood's ultimate 'secret' sound effect

items.text: In 1998 a deletion command nearly wiped out Toy Story 2, and about 90% of the film's files vanished. The backups had been failing, and the film was saved by a copy on its supervising technical director's home computer.
items.note: Accounts differ on the exact date and on what was deleted. Some Pixar staff say it was the database of master assets rather than finished frames.

sources.title: How Pixar recovered Toy Story 2 after a Unix command deleted nearly the entire film in 1998

items.text: On January 1, 2024, the early Mickey Mouse from the 1928 short Steamboat Willie entered the public domain in the U.S. for the first time.
items.note: Only the 1928 version of Mickey is free to use. Later versions of the character are still protected.

sources.title: 'Steamboat Willie': An early version of Mickey Mouse is now in the public domain

items.text: Steamboat Willie was once due to enter the public domain in 1985. Copyright law changes in 1976 and 1998 pushed that date back to 2024.
items.note: This describes U.S. law. Other countries have different rules, and the NYU source says the film has been public domain in Brazil since 1999.

sources.title: Steamboat Willie is in the Public Domain. What Does That Mean for Mickey Mouse?
sources.publisher: NYU Journal of Intellectual Property & Entertainment Law

items.text: Steamboat Willie, Mickey Mouse's public debut, was also one of the first animated short films with synchronized sound.
In Jurassic Park, the raptors' hissing was voiced by geese. When they bark to each other in the kitchen scene, you're hearing a recording of tortoises mating.
items.note: Sound designer Gary Rydstrom described this in an interview with Vulture. He recorded the tortoises at Marine World.

sources.title: The Raptor Noises in Jurassic Park Are Mating Tortoises

items.text: The roar of Jurassic Park's T. rex was built partly from a baby elephant and the sounds of the sound designer's Jack Russell terrier, Buster.
items.note: The roars were layered from many recordings. The dog and elephant were two of the sources.

sources.title: The Raptor Noises in Jurassic Park Are Mating Tortoises
Jurassic Bark: How Sound Design Changed Our Imaginations

items.text: Nobody knows what dinosaurs really sounded like. In Jurassic Park, the running Gallimimus herd was given the squeals of horses.
items.note: What dinosaurs really sounded like is unknown. The film's sounds are creative choices made by the sound team.

sources.title: Jurassic Bark: How Sound Design Changed Our Imaginations
The Raptor Noises in Jurassic Park Are Mating Tortoises

items.text: Hollywood actress Hedy Lamarr co-invented a 'frequency hopping' radio system with composer George Antheil. It was meant to stop radio-controlled torpedoes from being jammed, and they received a patent in 1942.
items.note: Frequency hopping is an ancestor of some modern wireless techniques. It isn't a single invention behind all of Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.

sources.title: Hedy Lamarr's WWII Invention Helped Shape Modern Tech

items.text: One of the original Wi-Fi standards, IEEE 802.11 from 1997, used frequency hopping. IEEE says it leveraged Hedy Lamarr's patent, which had expired in 1959.
items.note: Lamarr's patent is one ancestor of the technique. Wi-Fi was built by many engineers over time.

sources.title: Actress/Inventor Hedy Lamarr – and How Far Wireless Communication Has Come

items.text: The tornado in the 1939 Wizard of Oz was a cloth windsock about 35 feet long, like the ones at airports. It was spun and moved from a steel gantry above the stage.

sources.title: "Wizard of Oz" tornado scene remains a classic
Movie history: Wizard of Oz turns 75 Friday

items.text: The first legal U.S. TV commercial aired on July 1, 1941. It was a 10-second Bulova watch ad shown before a Dodgers–Phillies baseball game, and it cost the company just $9.
items.note: It is called the first 'legal' ad because some companies had aired unpaid test commercials earlier. Some sources give the length as 9 seconds and the cost as $4–$9.

sources.title: The First 'Legal' TV Commercial Aired 75 Years Ago Today
